about: Domino Effect shows a man in a light blue shirt crouching on a black mat and nudging the tiniest tile in a line of dominoes, each one noticeably bigger than the last, until the final slab towers far above his head. The picture explains the joke on its own: one little push is enough to bring down something enormous. In meme form the small domino is labelled with a harmless-looking action and the giant one with the huge consequence it eventually caused, often years later and in a way nobody could have predicted.
origin: The photo comes from a 2009 physics demonstration video by University of Toronto professor Stephen Morris, in which a chain of dominoes grows in size with every tile. Redditors started labelling the first and last pieces to show absurd chains of cause and effect.
usage:
The first box goes on the tiny domino the man is touching: a small, innocent cause such as a single decision, purchase or comment. The second box goes on the biggest domino: the massive outcome it set off.

The bigger the gap between the two, the better. A one-word cause next to a world-changing result is funnier than two medium-sized events. Personal histories (one YouTube video that became a career), history jokes and tech disasters (one missing semicolon that took down production) all fit naturally.
